content: Glandular cheilitis, also referred to as actinic cheilosis or sailor's lip, is a specific type of cheilitis that is considered the lip equivalent of actinic keratosis of the skin. This condition has the potential to progress into squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). In actinic cheilitis, the affected lip typically exhibits a thickened, whitish discoloration at the junction between the lip and the surrounding skin. The normally well-defined vermilion border, which separates the red portion of the lip from the adjacent skin, becomes blurred or indistinct. As the condition advances, the lip may develop scaling and induration. The lesion is generally painless and persistent. It is more frequently observed in older males and individuals with fair skin who have a history of chronic sun exposure. Causes Actinic cheilitis is primarily caused by prolonged and excessive exposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation from sunlight. Additional contributing factors may include tobacco use, chronic lip irritation, poor oral hygiene, and the use of ill-fitting dentures. Treatment Options Actinic cheilitis is considered a premalignant condition, as approximately 10% of cases may progress to squamous cell carcinoma. Since it is not possible to predict which lesions will become malignant, the current medical consensus is to treat all cases of actinic cheilitis. Treatment options aim to destroy or remove the damaged epithelium and include the following: Topical 5-fluorouracil (5-FU): This medication inhibits DNA synthesis, targeting rapidly dividing cells, which leads to their death. Normal skin is less affected. Treatment typically lasts 2–4 weeks and involves an inflammatory phase followed by redness, burning, oozing, and eventual erosion. Therapy is discontinued when ulceration and crusting appear. Scarring is minimal, and complete clearance is achieved in about 50% of patients. Imiquimod: This immune response modifier promotes an immune-mediated attack on tumor cells, leading to their apoptosis. It also activates T-cells and macrophages, resulting in epidermal erosion. Imiquimod may reduce lesion recurrence by promoting immune memory. Scarring is minimal, and clearance rates of up to 45% have been reported for actinic keratoses. However, optimal dosing and long-term efficacy for actinic cheilitis remain under investigation. Procedures Cryosurgery: This involves the application of liquid nitrogen using an open-spray technique. Local anesthesia is not required, but treating the entire lip can be painful. Cure rates exceed 96%, making it the preferred treatment for focal areas of actinic cheilitis. However, adjacent tissue damage may delay healing and promote scarring. Electrosurgery: This alternative method requires local anesthesia and is less practical than cryosurgery. Tissue damage can similarly delay healing and increase the risk of scarring. Shave Vermillionectomy: This procedure removes a portion of the vermilion ridge while preserving the underlying muscle. Significant bleeding may occur due to the vascular nature of the lip, and a linear scar may form, though this can often be minimized with massage and steroids. Healing is rapid, and the procedure is highly effective. Carbon Dioxide Laser Ablation: This technique ablates the vermilion border and is relatively quick and effective, though it requires a skilled operator and anesthesia. Secondary infection and scarring are possible but generally minimal and responsive to steroids. Pain during the healing phase, which can last three weeks or more, is a potential issue. The success rate is high, with minimal recurrence. Chemical Peeling: Using 50% trichloroacetic acid has been evaluated, but results are generally poor. Healing takes 7–10 days with few side effects, but success rates are reported to be below 30%. Each treatment method has its own advantages and limitations, and the choice of therapy depends on the extent of the lesion, patient preferences, and the clinician's expertise.
